UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                             BEFORE THE
               FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION



Southwest Power Pool, Inc.                    )       Docket No.      ER26-1323-000
                                              )



             MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER AND ANSWER OF
                    SOUTHWEST POWER POOL, INC.

       Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal

Energy Regulatory Commission (the “Commission” or “FERC”), 18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212

and 385.213, Southwest Power Pool, Inc. (“SPP”) submits this Motion for Leave to Answer

and Answer1 in response to the comments and protests filed in this proceeding.




1
       SPP respectfully requests leave to respond to the comments and protests filed in
       this proceeding to aid the Commission’s decision-making process. The
       Commission regularly permits answers for good cause shown, and the Commission
       has held that answers are permitted when they ensure a more accurate and complete
       record, clarify the issues, or provide useful and relevant information that will assist
       the Commission in its deliberative process. See, e.g., City Utils. of Springfield, Mo.
       v. Sw. Power Pool, Inc., 168 FERC ¶ 61,085, at P 51 (2019) (“We accept the
       answers . . . because they have provided information that assisted us in our
       decision-making process.”), order on reh’g & clarification, 170 FERC ¶ 61,024
       (2020); Sw. Power Pool, Inc., 144 FERC ¶ 61,059, at P 17 (2013) (same) order on
       reh’g & compliance, 149 FERC ¶ 61,048 (2014), order on reh’g & compliance
       filing, 151 FERC ¶ 61,045 (2015), petition for review dismissed sub nom. LSP
       Transmission Holdings, LLC v. FERC, 700 F. App’x 1 (D.C. Cir. 2017) (per
       curiam); Morgan Stanley Capital Grp., Inc. v. N.Y. Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 93
       FERC ¶ 61,017, at 61,036 (2000) (accepting an answer as “helpful in the
       development of the record”). SPP’s silence on statements contained in comments
       or protests should not be considered agreement or acquiescence to any unaddressed
       conclusions or statements.
 I.     BACKGROUND

       On February 10, 2026, SPP submitted revisions to its Open Access Transmission

Tariff2 to add the proposed Conditional High Impact Large Load Service (“CHILLS”) that

will allow High Impact Large Loads (“HILL”) to be served with non-firm conditional

Transmission Service.3

       Several parties filed motions to intervene.4




2
       Southwest Power Pool, Inc., Open Access Transmission Tariff, Sixth Revised
       Volume No. 1 (“Tariff”). References in this answer to “Tariff” refer to the version
       of SPP’s Tariff currently in effect. “Proposed Tariff” refers to a version reflecting
       revisions proposes in this proceeding. All capitalized terms not otherwise defined
       in this answer shall have the definitions assigned by the Tariff.
3
       Submission of Tariff Revisions to Add Conditional High Impact Large Load
       Service of Southwest Power Pool, Inc., Docket No. ER26-1323-000 (Feb. 10, 2026)
       (“CHILLS Filing”).
4
       Interventions were filed by: Advanced Energy United; Basin Electric Power
       Cooperative; Constellation Energy Generation, LLC; Electric Power Supply
       Association; Enchanted Rock, LLC; Geronimo Power, LLC; Kansas Electric
       Power Cooperative, Inc.; Louisiana Public Service Commission; Municipal Energy
       Agency of Nebraska; Omaha Public Power District; Public Citizen, Inc.; Solar
       Energy Industries Association; Southwest Power Pool Market Monitoring Unit;
       Southwest Power Pool Transmission Owner Group (comprised of American
       Electric Power Service Corporation; Evergy Kansas Central, Inc., Evergy Metro,
       Inc., and Evergy Missouri West, Inc.; Oklahoma Gas and Electric Company, and
       Xcel Energy Services Inc.); Sunflower Electric Power Corporation; Western Area
       Power Administration; Western Farmers Electric Cooperative.

                                             2
        Advanced Energy United,5 ITC Great Plains, LLC,6 the Solar Energy Industries

Association,7 and the Southwest Power Pool Transmission Owner Group8 filed comments

in support of the CHILLS Filing.

       The Southwest Power Pool Market Monitoring Unit (“MMU”) filed comments

stating it takes no position regarding the necessity of SPP’s proposal, but it finds that the

proposal incorporates CHILLS in a manner that is fair and efficient.9

       Associated Electric Power Cooperative, Inc. (“AECI”) filed comments regarding

the impact of CHILLS on affected systems, coordination between SPP and affected system

operators, and the proposed Curtailment procedures.10

       Enchanted Rock, LLC filed a limited protest regarding proposed language that is

applicable during Emergency Conditions and other specified circumstances (the

“Emergency Override Provisions”).11




5
       Comments of Advanced Energy United, Docket No. ER26-1323-000 (Mar. 3,
       2026).
6
       Motion to Intervene and Supporting Comments of ITC Great Plains, LLC, Docket
       No. ER26-1323-000 (Mar. 3, 2026).
7
       Comments of the Solar Energy Industries Association in Support, Docket No.
       ER26-1323-000 (Mar. 3, 2026).
8
       Comments of the Southwest Power Pool Transmission Owner Group, Docket No.
       ER26-1323-000 (Mar. 3, 2026).
9
       Comments of the Southwest Power Pool Market Monitoring Unit, Docket No.
       ER26-1323-000 (Mar. 3, 2026) (“MMU Comments”).
10
       Motion to Intervene and Comments of Associated Electric Cooperative, Inc.,
       Docket No. ER26-1323-000 (Mar. 3, 2026) (“AECI Comments”).
11
       Limited Protest of Enchanted Rock, LLC, Docket No. ER26-1323-000 (Mar. 3,
       2026) (“Enchanted Rock Protest”).

                                             3
 II.    ANSWER

       A.      Answer to Enchanted Rock

       Enchanted Rock states that it “is generally supportive of the CHILLS Proposal,”

but it protests SPP’s proposed addition to Attachment AE, Section 2.22.2(2)(b). Enchanted

Rock contends that this provision would force backup generation to unjustly serve the

broader market and exacerbate fuel related challenges for the Resources supporting HILLs.

Enchanted Rock claims these provisions “cause SPP’s entire proposed market and

reliability construct to collapse at the very moment it is most needed.”

       SPP’s proposal for this Tariff section reads as follows:

       Resources with Load Limited Resource Interconnection Service as defined
       in Attachment BB of the Tariff must: [e]nsure the sum of the Maximum
       Economic Capacity Operating Limits of supporting Resources with Load
       Limited Resource Interconnection Service, as defined in Attachment BB of
       the Tariff, does not exceed the submitted HILL or CHILL load forecast
       value of the corresponding HILL or CHILL except when directed by the
       Transmission Provider to mitigate Emergency Conditions or as specified in
       the Resource’s generator interconnection agreement.12

       This provision creates a general rule that caps the ability of Resources with Load

Limited Resource Interconnection Service (“LLRIS”) to inject power into the

Transmission System at the load forecast value of the load they are supporting. It allows

for two possible exceptions to the injection cap. The first is when directed by the

Transmission Provider, i.e., SPP, to mitigate Emergency Conditions, and the second is

when specified in the Resource’s generator interconnection agreement.

       Enchanted Rock’s description of the effect of this language is misleading. First, it

does not create a special compulsion to sell power to the market beyond that of other



12
       CHILLS Filing at Proposed Tariff, Attachment AE, Section 2.22.2(2)(b).

                                             4
 interconnected generation. Second, it does not prevent the CHILL from operating, it simply

curtails its ability to withdraw power from the Transmission System. If the Resource has a

way to supply the load it supports without using the Transmission System, it can continue

to do so, but the load must cease to withdraw from the Transmission System.

       SPP’s first exception is just and reasonable as it allows SPP to temporarily treat

generation with LLRIS like other Resources in limited circumstances to maintain

reliability. LLRIS is only granted on a five-year basis. If a Resource with LLRIS wishes to

remain interconnected, the Resource must submit a separate Interconnection Request

through SPP’s standard generator interconnection process. Although Resources do not

have the same study requirements to receive the service that Resources with Network

Resource Interconnection Service (“NRIS”) or Energy Resource Connection Service

(“ERIS”) do, those studies will likely be ongoing during the period a Resource has LLRIS.

During the LLRIS term, SPP will gain knowledge of the effects of power injections by that

Resource to the Transmission System. If Emergency Conditions arise, it is just and

reasonable to give SPP some discretion to allow injections it would not normally allow to

mitigate Emergency Conditions. It is not unduly discriminatory to allow the Resources to

help mitigate an emergency if they are available and it is reliable to do so. Furthermore,

SPP’s Tariff does not allow any special rights to use the Transmission System for particular

Resources to support particular loads. The lack of Tariff provisions allowing LLRIS

Resources the right to support CHILLs under all conditions does not make SPP’s proposal

unduly discriminatory or preferential.

       SPP’s second proposed exception, “specified in the Resource’s generator

interconnection agreement,” does not itself create an exception, it only clarifies that there

is not a Tariff conflict if this exception is allowed through a separate agreement.
                                             5
        SPP specifically disagrees with the statement that

       A fundamental purpose of the CHILLS framework is to ensure that, during
       transmission constraints or emergencies, the supporting HILLGA Resource
       remains available to serve the curtailed CHILLS Customer, allowing the
       CHILLS Customer to continue meeting its own power needs from its
       dedicated generation rather than face the risk of a total shutdown.13

       On the contrary, CHILLs may specifically have their transmission service curtailed,

which means that their withdrawals from the Transmission System must cease.14 Ensuring

the availability of Resources to support CHILLs is not fundamental to SPP’s proposal, and

SPP does not propose to grant HILLGAs and CHILLs superior rights to deliver or to

receive power over the Transmission System over the rights allowed other loads and

Resources. If it is critical for these loads to have continuous power, including during

Emergency Conditions, the CHILL must have access to generation or storage that does not

require use of the Transmission System. Using backup generation to serve onsite load in

the event the load has its conditional Transmission Service curtailed is not forbidden by

the SPP Tariff, so long as the generation is not using the Transmission System to do so.

Finally, CHILLS is a limited Transmission Service that may be curtailed in Emergency

Conditions, and LLRIS is a limited Resource interconnection service. SPP may choose not

to curtail all CHILLS in the event of Emergency Conditions,15 and SPP should be able to



13
       Enchanted Rock Protest at 6.
14
       SPP defines Curtailment in the Tariff’s Common Service Provisions as “[a]
       reduction in firm or non-firm transmission service in response to a transmission
       capacity shortage as a result of system reliability conditions.”
15
       For example, a CHILL may interconnect to the Transmission System at a point
       where its continued operation is providing reliability benefits by reducing loading
       on a flowgate. Under those conditions, SPP may find that it is beneficial to
       reliability to allow that particular CHILL to continue to withdraw from the
       Transmission System.

                                            6
 similarly relax the prohibition on net injections to allow Resources with LLRIS to help

maintain reliability when appropriate. SPP’s proposed limited exceptions to the injection

cap for Resources with LLRIS are just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory.

       B.      Response to MMU

               i.     MMU Recommendations

       The MMU outlines eight (8) recommendations to the CHILLS proposal.

Specifically, the MMU recommends the following: (1) CHILLS curtailment be initiated

prior to Reliability Registered Demand Response Resources, which are a specific type of

demand response resource that will be proposed to the Commission in a future filing; (2)

document in the Tariff and Market Protocols a statement that SPP will only commit

reliability status resources or make local reliability commitments to supply firm load; (3)

SPP monitor for CHILLs becoming uncovered over time and, if necessary, reassess the

CHILLS framework considering those findings; (4) SPP implement oversight mechanisms

to ensure CHILLs continue to be evaluated for sufficiency for long term resource adequacy

and do not represent an unmanaged risk; (5) resources designated to support a CHILL

should be expressly barred from being designated as a System Support Resource; (6) SPP

produce additional documentation to improve transparency and consistency, including (i)

how SPP will evaluate and rely on information about runtime-limited resources and (ii)

any standards applicable to run-time-limited resources dedicated to CHILLs; (7)

implement strong incentives for CHILLs to respond to curtailment instructions; and (8)

SPP incentivize CHILLs, HILLs, and nonconforming loads to provide accurate operational

load forecasts.16


16
       MMU Comments at 2-3.

                                            7
        SPP was made aware of these recommendations by the MMU during the

development of the CHILLS proposal. SPP has committed to the MMU to continue to work

on these recommendations and implement those deemed necessary to continue to reliably

operate the Transmission System with the provision of CHILLS.

       Although SPP has committed to working with the MMU on these

recommendations, these recommendations are not proffered in the MMU Comments as

reasons for the Commission to reject the CHILLS Filing as unjust, unreasonable, or unduly

discriminatory or preferential.17 The Commission should not determine the just and

reasonableness of the CHILLS proposal based upon preferred recommendations of the

MMU, but instead, the Commission must only make that determination based upon the just

and reasonableness of the proposal before it.18 The Commission should accept the CHILLS

Filing to the extent that it determines the filing to be just and reasonable.19




17
       See MMU Comments at 5 (“The MMU takes no position on the necessity of SPP’s
       proposal. If the Commission does find SPP’s proposal is necessary, the MMU finds
       that the proposal incorporates CHILLS in a matter that is fair and efficient, and the
       Commission should approve the proposal as a just and reasonable way to effectuate
       SPP’s goals.”)
18
       See, e.g., Oxy USA, Inc. v. FERC, 64 F.3d 679, 692 (D.C. Cir. 1995) (stating that a
       proposal under FPA section 205 “need not be the only reasonable methodology, or
       even the most accurate”); Louisville Gas & Elec. Co., 114 FERC ¶ 61,282, at P 29
       (“[T]he just and reasonable standard under the FPA is not so rigid as to limit rates
       to a ‘best rate’ or ‘most efficient rate’ standard. Rather, a range of alternative
       approaches often may be just and reasonable.”), order on reh’g sub nom. E.ON U.S.
       LLC, 116 FERC ¶ 61,020 (2006).
19
       16 U.S.C. § 824d; Advanced Energy Mgmt. All. v. FERC, 860 F.3d 656, 662 (D.C.
       Cir. 2017) (“When acting on a public utility's rate filing under section 205, the
       Commission undertakes ‘an essentially passive and reactive role’ and restricts itself
       to evaluating the confined proposal.” (quoting City of Winnfield v. FERC, 744 F.2d
       871, 875-76 (D.C. Cir. 1984)).

                                               8
         ii.     MMU’s Claimed Error in the Calculation of Network Load

        The MMU claims that it has identified a perceived error with how SPP describes

the calculation for the adjustment to Network Load when there is a CHILL, Network Load,

and a generator capable of producing excess generation all located at the same point of

interconnection. Specifically, the MMU points to Section 17.0 of the Conditional High

Impact Large Load Service Agreement (“CHILLSA”) which states: “[T]he Network Load

must be adjusted for any excess hourly generation above the CHILLS Reserved Capacity.

Such excess hourly generation will be calculated as the minimum of the CHILLS load and

the CHILLS Reserved Capacity, plus the hourly generation amount, less the CHILLS

Reserved Capacity.”20

        The purpose of this described calculation, as pointed out in the MMU Comments,21

is to describe how that Network Load should be calculated for settlement purposes in

situations where there is Behind-The-Meter Generation located at the same Point of

Delivery as Network Load and CHILLS load to prevent any netting of loads reported for

Network Integration Transmission Service. This treatment is consistent with how other

Network Load is prevented from netting when located at the same delivery point as Behind-

The-Meter Generation.

        Upon review of this calculation in Section 17.0 of the CHILLSA, SPP has

determined that, even though it does not agree that there is an error in the stated calculation,

the description of the calculation may cause confusion. SPP’s intent is to ensure that




20
        CHILLS Filing at Proposed Tariff, Attachment BA, Addendum 1, Section 17.0.
21
        MMU Comments at 3.

                                               9
 Network Load is calculated consistent with the Tariff and is not improperly netted due to

the presence of a generator at the same Point of Interconnection.

       To remedy this possible confusion, and if so ordered by the Commission on

compliance, SPP will refile that Tariff sheet without the final sentence of the section that

lays out the calculation.

       SPP’s potential edits to Section 17.0 of the CHILLSA are as follows:

       The Transmission Customer’s or Network Customer’s CHILLS load will
       be measured on an hourly integrated basis, by suitable metering equipment
       located at each connection and delivery point. The CHILLS load will be a
       separately metered quantity, apart from any firm load served at the same
       point of delivery. Any generation located at the same point of delivery will
       be metered separately from the CHILLS load and separately from any firm
       load at the same point of delivery. The meter owner must cause to be
       provided to the Transmission Provider, Transmission Customer or Network
       Customer and applicable Transmission Owner, such data as required by
       Transmission Provider for billing. The Transmission Customer’s or
       Network Customer’s load must be adjusted, for settlement purposes, to
       include applicable transmission and distribution losses. Measurements
       taken and all metering equipment must be in accordance with the
       Transmission Provider’s standards and practices for similarly determining
       Network Load under the Tariff. The actual hourly CHILLS load and any
       firm load, by delivery point, internal generation site, and point where power
       may flow to or from the Transmission Customer or Network Customer, with
       separate readings for each direction of flow, must be provided. For instances
       where both Network Load and CHILLS load are located at the same point
       of delivery with Behind-The-Meter Generation, as defined in Attachment
       AE of the Tariff, the Network Load must be adjusted for any excess hourly
       generation above the CHILLS Reserved Capacity. Such excess hourly
       generation will be calculated as the minimum of the CHILLS load and the
       CHILLS Reserved Capacity, plus the hourly generation amount, less the
       CHILLS Reserved Capacity.


       SPP’s filing is just and reasonable without this sentence as the intent of the

language, i.e., to adjust the Network Load to account for excess generation, is still clear in

the remainder of Section 17.0 of the CHILLSA. The CHILL and the generation must both




                                             10
 have dedicated metering,22 but the Tariff does not mandate this for Network Load. As a

result, SPP may need to make clarifying edits to the SPP Business Practices to ensure that

the metered values properly account for Network Load. As the exact nature of this

adjustment can vary with the metering configuration, the exact formula for this calculation

is an implementation detail not required to be in the Tariff. SPP will make this change,

deleting the final sentence of Section 17.0, if so ordered.

       C.      Answer to AECI

       AECI states that the CHILLS Filing fails to provide sufficient details concerning

(1) how SPP plans to coordinate with “Affected System Owners” during the CHILLS

interconnection process and (2) the mechanics of curtailing CHILLs.23 Although SPP

appreciates AECI’s interest in this proceeding as a neighboring transmission provider, the

Tariff and the CHILLS Filing already account for AECI’s concerns and, further, AECI’s

requested enhancements are implementation details not within the Commission’s role in

reviewing the CHILLS Filing under Section 205 of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”).

       As a general matter, SPP is not required to justify not including certain features in

its proposal that third parties might prefer.24 To be just and reasonable, SPP’s proposed


22
       Attachment AE, section 2.5 and CHILLS Filing Proposed Tariff Attachment AE,
       section 2.22.1(b)(2).
23
       AECI Comments at 3.
24
       See, e.g., Neb. Pub. Power Dist. v. FERC, 957 F.3d. 932, 943 (8th. Cir. 2020)
       (stating that the law does not require the Commission to consider alternative
       suggests, but only whether the rate proposal itself is just and reasonable (citations
       omitted); Cities of Bethany v. FERC, 727 F.2d 1131, 1136 (D.C. Cir. 1984) (finding
       that the Commission properly did not consider “whether a proposed rate schedule
       is more or less reasonable than alternative rate designs”); Sw. Power Pool, Inc., 182
       FERC ¶ 61,141, at P 115 (“Because we affirm the Presiding Judge’s finding that
       SPP’s proposal is just and reasonable, we need not consider whether the proposal

                                             11
 revisions must only be found to be within a “zone of reasonableness.”25 The Commission’s

role in reviewing the CHILLS Filing is “essentially passive and reactive” and confined to

considering the proposal as submitted by SPP.26 The Commission should therefore accept

the CHILLS Filing as just and reasonable and should reject AECI’s requests proposed in

its comments.

       Nothing within the proposed CHILLS Filing changes how SPP does or will

coordinate with neighboring transmission providers when studying new load additions or

modifications. SPP currently monitors neighboring transmission provider systems in its

study processes for new load additions and modifications and will continue to do so with

the CHILLS study process. SPP allows neighbors to perform affected system studies as

necessary. A CHILLS customer will be required to coordinate with the neighboring

transmission provider(s) to resolve any identified issues caused by the new load addition

or modification, which is what is required for current Transmission Customers.27 AECI’s




       is more or less reasonable than other alternatives.” (citations omitted), order on
       reh’g, 184 FERC ¶ 61,004 (2023); Midwest Indep. Transmission Sys. Operator,
       Inc., 131 FERC ¶ 61,185, at P 25 (2010) (“[T]he mere fact that the methodology
       can be refined does not undercut [the Commission’s] conclusion that [a proposed]
       method affords a just and reasonable rate for transmission customers. As the court
       noted . . . ‘reasonableness is a zone, not a pinpoint.’” (citation omitted)).
25
       See Indep. Power Producers of New York, Inc. v. FERC, No. 21-1166, 2022 WL
       3210362, at *2 (D.C. Cir. Aug. 9, 2022) (unpublished) (“A ‘just and reasonable rate
       is one that falls within’ a ‘zone of reasonableness.’”) (internal citation omitted).
26
       See Advanced Energy Mgmt. All. v. FERC, 860 F.3d 656, 662 (D.C. Cir. 2017)
       (stating “[w]hen acting on a public utility’s rate filing under section 205, the
       Commission undertakes ‘an essentially passive and reactive role’ and restricts itself
       to evaluating the confined proposal.” (quoting City of Winnfield v. FERC, 774 F.2d
       871, 875-76 (D.C. Cir. 1984)).
27
       See Tariff, Part II, Sections 16.2 and 21; Part III, Section 29.3; and Attachment BA,
       Section 2.1.3.4. See also CHILLS Filing at Proposed Tariff, Part VII, Section 47.3

                                            12
 concerns about how SPP will coordinate with third party affected transmission providers

are already addressed in the Tariff and by language proposed in the CHILLS Filing.

       AECI requests that the Commission direct SPP to implement a standardized

framework for the curtailment of CHILLS and a mechanism for physical control of HILLs

by Transmission Operators. The conditions for CHILLS Curtailment are part of SPP’s

proposed Tariff changes.28 SPP is currently working on the implementation details for the

mechanics of CHILL Curtailments. This includes initiatives responding to the MMU’s

concerns, considering the appropriate response for a failure to comply with instructions to

reduce CHILL load, and considering appropriate integration into the SPP Emergency

Operations Plan. SPP’s proposed Tariff changes are just and reasonable without including

details of Curtailment procedures and mechanisms of physical control.




28
       See CHILLS Filing at Proposed Tariff, Attachment AE, Section 2.22.1(c)-(d).

                                            13
 III.     CONCLUSION

         SPP respectfully requests that the Commission accept this Answer to assist the

Commission in its decision-making process, find that the CHILLS Filing is just and

reasonable, and issue an order accepting the CHILLS Filing.
